quote: The Second Law of Thermodynamics is a corollary of Liouville’s Theorem
content: It is not, and the reason it is not is the entire content of the foundations of statistical mechanics. Liouville’s theorem is time-reversal symmetric; it therefore cannot by itself distinguish the past from the future, and any argument from phase-space conservation to entropy increase works equally well run backward to give entropy increase toward the past (Loschmidt’s objection, 1876). To get the Second Law one needs, in addition, a low-entropy boundary condition on the early universe, the “Past Hypothesis” (Albert, Time and Chance, 2000, a book with no DOI; Callender (1999)), plus a coarse-graining or typicality assumption whose justification is disputed (Earman (2006) argues the Past Hypothesis is not even well-formed in general relativity). The essay gestures at the coarse-graining (“squiggles and wiggles”) and never mentions the initial condition at all, which is where the explanatory work is. Also, Liouville’s theorem is a result of classical Hamiltonian mechanics; the “standard model of physics” is a quantum field theory in which the analogous statement is unitarity, and the classical phase-space picture the essay draws is an approximation to it, not a theorem within it.

quote: A bit of physics occurred, and lo, the entropy of Y went to 0, but the entropy of X went to log2(7) = 2.8 bits.
content: The essay’s own table maps four states into X2, X4, X6 and X8, so X’s entropy after the interaction is exactly 2 bits, and the total entropy is conserved, as Liouville requires. The essay gets 2.8 bits by declining to read its own four-line table (“it would be too costly to think out exactly which states”) and then presents the resulting increase as an illustration of the Second Law. This is the objection to the subjectivist account in miniature: on the essay’s view, the entropy of a system went up by 0.8 bits because the author was lazy, and the water in the refrigerator is correspondingly warmer. Jaynes had an answer (the experimental entropy is the information entropy of the macrostate one has chosen to control, and one is not free to choose arbitrarily), but the essay does not give it, and the example as written shows a quantity that changes with the bookkeeper’s effort being identified with a quantity that a thermometer measures.

quote: Ignoring quantumness for the moment, the answer is: Yes! Yes it is!
content: The thermometer disagrees. After Laplace’s revelation the mean kinetic energy of the molecules is unchanged, heat still flows from the glass into a colder body at the same rate, and every calorimetric measurement returns the same entropy as before; what has changed is that an agent with a memory large enough to hold the microstate could in principle extract work. The generalized Second Law makes the accounting explicit: the work extractable is bounded by the free-energy drop plus kT times the mutual information between the memory and the system (Sagawa & Ueda (2008)), and the memory must be reset at Landauer cost before the demon can operate again. For a glass of water that is roughly 1025 molecules times several bits each; the demon’s memory carries more entropy than the water did, and the joint system’s entropy has not gone down. So the claim “the water is cold in a genuinely thermodynamic sense” is true only of the water-plus-demon system under an idealization in which the demon is free, and the essay reports it as a fact about the water. The philosophical dispute over whether the information-theoretic exorcism of the demon is even non-circular (Earman & Norton (1998), Norton (2011)) is not mentioned; the essay writes as if the matter were closed by Szilárd in 1929.

quote: (It is sometimes said that it is erasing bits in order to prepare for the next observation that takes the thermodynamic work—but that distinction is just a matter of words and perspective; the math is unambiguous.)
content: The parenthesis waves away the central result of the field, and the result contradicts the essay’s moral. Bennett (1982) showed that measurement, the acquisition of mutual information with a system, can be carried out reversibly at zero thermodynamic cost; the unavoidable cost, kT ln 2 per bit (Landauer (1961)), is paid only on erasure. This is not a matter of perspective: it determines that a demon with a large blank memory can extract work for as long as the memory lasts, that the work is repaid only when the memory is cleared, and that the two steps can be separated by an arbitrary interval. Both halves were later measured, the erasure cost by Bérut et al. (2012) and information-to-work conversion by Toyabe et al. (2010). The essay’s sentence “one subsystem cannot increase in mutual information with another subsystem, without (a) interacting with it and (b) doing thermodynamic work” is therefore false at (b); observing is free, forgetting is what costs. The essay’s slogan “to form accurate beliefs about something, you really do have to observe it” survives, since (a) is right, but the thermodynamic wrapper around it is wrong in the one place the physics is specific.

quote: For example, to the extent that an engine of cognition is not perfectly efficient, it must radiate waste heat, just like a car engine or refrigerator.
content: The analogy conflates two efficiencies. Thermodynamic inefficiency in a computer is logical irreversibility, the erasure of bits, and it has no relation to epistemic inefficiency, the failure to update correctly on evidence: a perfectly Bayesian updater implemented with irreversible gates radiates heat, and a hopelessly biased one implemented reversibly radiates none. The bound is also irrelevant at the scale of any actual mind. A human brain dissipates about 20 watts, on the order of 1021 kT per second, and the measured metabolic cost of transmitting one bit at a synapse is around 104 ATP molecules, or 105 to 106 kT per bit (Laughlin, de Ruyter van Steveninck & Anderson (1998)), six orders of magnitude above the Landauer limit. The Second Law constrains cognition in the way it constrains a bonfire: it is true, and it explains nothing about the design. The essay’s real claim, that you cannot get evidence without contact with the world, is a claim about correlation, and it needed no thermodynamics; wrapping it in Liouville, Szilárd and Jaynes lends it the authority of physics without any of the physics doing work.
